o: It is C3, C4 and C5, mainly C4

The phrenic nerve is C3, C4 and C5, mainly C4. Diaphragmatic muscle migrated from cervical myotomes into the septum transversum, bringing its nerve with it.
"C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive."
It descends on scalenus anterior deep to the prevertebral fascia

The phrenic nerve descends on scalenus anterior deep to the prevertebral fascia. The transverse cervical and suprascapular arteries cross it in front of the fascia.
The fascia protects it in superficial neck surgery.
The right phrenic nerve passes through the oesophageal opening of the diaphragm

The right phrenic nerve passes through the vena caval opening in the central tendon (T8). The left pierces the muscle of the left dome.
Neither uses the oesophageal opening.
It is accompanied by the pericardiacophrenic artery because it has no regional artery in the mediastinum

The phrenic nerve takes its own artery, the pericardiacophrenic, because there is no regional artery along its mediastinal course.
A branch of the internal thoracic artery.

questions.s: Sensory fibres of the phrenic nerve supply the:
o: Costal pleura

The costal pleura is supplied by the intercostal nerves, not the phrenic nerve.
Pain from it is felt locally on the chest wall.
Fibrous pericardium and parietal serous pericardium

About a third of phrenic fibres are sensory, supplying the fibrous pericardium and parietal serous pericardium.
Pericarditis can therefore cause shoulder-tip pain.
Visceral serous pericardium

Last's says the visceral serous pericardium (epicardium) is insensitive.
Like visceral pleura, it has no pain fibres.
Central parts of the diaphragmatic pleura and peritoneum

The phrenic nerve supplies the central parts of the diaphragmatic pleura and peritoneum; the periphery is supplied by the lower intercostal nerves.
Central irritation refers to the shoulder (C4). Answer B: 2 and 4.

questions.s: Regarding the vagi in the thorax:
o: The right vagus is in contact with the trachea

Last's says the vagi try to reach the midline. The right vagus lies on the trachea; on the left the great arteries hold the nerve away.
So the right vagus is in contact with the trachea.
The left vagus crosses the arch of the aorta deep to the left superior intercostal vein

On the left, the vagus crosses the aortic arch deep to the left superior intercostal vein, with the phrenic nerve anterior and the vein crossing between.
The phrenic is anterior, the vagus posterior.
Both vagi pass behind the lung roots

Both vagi pass behind the lung roots, contributing to the posterior pulmonary plexuses.
The phrenic nerves pass in front.
The anterior vagal trunk consists predominantly of right vagal fibres

The anterior vagal trunk consists mainly of left vagal fibres and the posterior trunk mainly of right, reflecting rotation of the gut.
"LARP": left anterior, right posterior.
The superficial part lies in front of the ligamentum arteriosum

The superficial part of the cardiac plexus lies in front of the ligamentum arteriosum; the deep part lies to its right, in front of the left main bronchus (and tracheal bifurcation).
The superficial part is small.
The superficial part receives the cardiac branch of the left superior cervical sympathetic ganglion

The superficial part receives the cardiac branch of the left superior cervical sympathetic ganglion and the inferior cervical cardiac branch of the left vagus.
All other cardiac branches go to the deep part.
Both recurrent laryngeal nerves contribute to the deep part

Both recurrent laryngeal nerves give cardiac branches to the deep cardiac plexus.
The deep plexus receives most of the cardiac nerves.
Cardiac pain fibres travel with the vagus

Cardiac pain travels with sympathetic fibres (cell bodies in upper thoracic dorsal root ganglia). Vagal afferents mediate cardiovascular reflexes.
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.
It lies on the necks of the ribs, anterior to the intercostal vessels and nerves

The thoracic sympathetic trunk lies on the necks of the ribs, anterior to the intercostal vessels and nerves, lateral to the heads of the ribs.
Lower down it moves onto the sides of the vertebral bodies.
The greater splanchnic nerve arises from the fifth to ninth ganglia

The greater splanchnic nerve arises from the fifth to ninth thoracic ganglia; the lesser from T10 and T11; the least from T12.
They carry preganglionic fibres to the abdomen.
It enters the abdomen behind the lateral arcuate ligament

The sympathetic trunk enters the abdomen behind the medial arcuate ligament, on the front of psoas. The subcostal bundle passes behind the lateral arcuate ligament.
Medial for the trunk, lateral for the subcostal nerve.
The least splanchnic nerve relays in a renal ganglion

Last's says the least splanchnic nerve relays in a renal ganglion, an offshoot of the coeliac ganglion behind the renal artery.
It supplies the kidney.
White rami communicantes are found on all cervical nerves

White rami communicantes exist only from T1 to L2; every spinal nerve receives a grey ramus, but cervical nerves have no white rami.
White rami carry the sympathetic outflow.
Removal of the T1 ganglion risks Horner's syndrome

Last's says never remove the T1 ganglion in upper limb sympathectomy, because it carries the outflow to the head and risks Horner's syndrome.
The T2 and T3 ganglia are removed instead.
Sympathetic fibres to the upper limb reach it mainly by running along the subclavian and axillary arteries

Last's says limb vessels get their sympathetic fibres from the adjacent peripheral nerves along their length, not from fibres running long distances along the arteries.
So arterial stripping is ineffective.
Removal of the L1 ganglion may compromise ejaculation

The L1 ganglion supplies the ductus deferens and seminal vesicles, so its removal may compromise ejaculation.
Answer B: 2 and 4.
The neurovascular bundle lies between the internal intercostal and innermost intercostal layers

The intercostal neurovascular bundle lies in the plane between the internal intercostal and innermost intercostal layers.
The same plane as the abdominal wall nerves.
From above down, the order in the costal groove is vein, artery, nerve

From above down, the order in the costal groove is vein, artery, nerve (VAN). The nerve lies lowest and is least protected.
So needles are inserted just above a rib.
The first intercostal nerve gives a large lateral cutaneous branch

Last's says the first intercostal nerve has no lateral or anterior cutaneous branch; most of it joins the brachial plexus.
The second intercostal gives the intercostobrachial nerve.
Levatores costarum are supplied by posterior rami

Last's says the levatores costarum are the only thoracic wall muscles supplied by posterior rami.
The intercostals are supplied by anterior rami.

questions.s: The posterior intercostal arteries of the first two spaces arise from the:
o: Superior intercostal artery

The posterior intercostal arteries of the first two spaces arise from the superior intercostal artery, a branch of the costocervical trunk (second part of the subclavian).
It descends in front of the neck of the first rib.
Internal thoracic artery

The internal thoracic artery gives the anterior intercostal arteries of the upper six spaces, not the posterior arteries of the first two.
Anterior and posterior arteries anastomose in each space.
Musculophrenic branch of the internal thoracic artery

The musculophrenic artery gives anterior intercostal branches to spaces 7 to 9.
It runs along the costal margin.
Descending thoracic aorta

The descending thoracic aorta supplies the posterior intercostal arteries of the remaining nine spaces (3 to 11).
Answer A: 1 only.
The radiate ligament has three bands, the central one forming the hypochordal bow

The radiate ligament of the costovertebral joint has three bands; Last's says the central one corresponds to the hypochordal bow.
This explains the anterior arch of the atlas.
The first rib articulates with C7 and T1

Last's says the first rib articulates with T1 only, never with C7.
Its head has a single facet.
The 11th and 12th ribs have no costotransverse synovial joints

The 11th and 12th ribs have no tubercles and no costotransverse synovial joints, only ligamentous attachments.
They are "floating ribs".
Every costochondral joint is a primary cartilaginous joint

Every costochondral joint is a primary cartilaginous joint; no movement occurs there.
The rib and its cartilage are continuous.
The subclavian artery lies in the groove on the upper surface, in contact with the bone

Last's says the lower trunk of the brachial plexus lies in the groove on the upper surface of the first rib. The subclavian artery usually lies a little higher, touching only the outer border.
A cervical rib compresses the lower trunk.
Scalenus medius inserts into the scalene tubercle

Scalenus anterior inserts into the scalene tubercle. Scalenus medius inserts behind the groove, between it and the tubercle of the rib.
The groove lies between the two scalenes.
The first costal cartilage forms a synovial joint with the manubrium

The first costal cartilage forms a primary cartilaginous joint with the manubrium, so the first ribs and manubrium move as one unit.
The second to seventh are synovial.
The subclavian vein lies in contact with the bone in front of the scalene tubercle

The subclavian vein lies in contact with the bone in its own groove in front of the scalene tubercle, in front of scalenus anterior.
Answer D: 4 only.

questions.s: Concerning the openings in the diaphragm:
o: The aortic opening lies at T12 behind the median arcuate ligament

The aortic opening lies at T12 behind the median arcuate ligament. It transmits the aorta, the azygos vein and the thoracic duct.
Strictly it is behind the diaphragm, not through it.
The oesophageal opening at T10 transmits the vagal trunks

The oesophageal opening at T10 transmits the oesophagus, the vagal trunks and the oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels.
It is surrounded by right crus fibres.
The vena caval opening lies in the left leaf of the central tendon

The vena caval opening lies near the junction of the central and right leaves of the central tendon, at T8, not in the left leaf.
The right phrenic nerve passes through it too.
The splanchnic nerves pierce the crura

The greater, lesser and least splanchnic nerves pierce the crura of the diaphragm to reach the coeliac plexus.
The sympathetic trunk passes behind the medial arcuate ligament.
Septum transversum

The septum transversum forms the central tendon of the diaphragm.
It originally lay in the neck, explaining the cervical nerve supply.
Pleuroperitoneal membranes

The pleuroperitoneal membranes contribute; their failure is the commonest cause of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (Bochdalek, posterolateral).
Usually on the left.
Third to fifth cervical myotomes

Muscle cells from the third to fifth cervical myotomes migrate into the diaphragm, bringing the phrenic nerve with them.
Hence C3, 4, 5.
Dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus and body wall mesoderm

The dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus (forming the crura) and body wall mesoderm (the periphery) also contribute. Last's lists all four sources.
All four true: E.

questions.s: Regarding the nerve supply of the pleura and lungs:
o: The parietal pleura of the chest wall is supplied by the intercostal nerves

The parietal pleura of the chest wall is supplied by the intercostal nerves and is pain-sensitive.
Pleurisy causes sharp, localised chest wall pain.
The visceral pleura has only autonomic supply and is insensitive

The visceral pleura has only autonomic (vasomotor) supply and no pain fibres, so it is insensitive.
Lung disease is painless until the parietal pleura is involved.
Sympathetic fibres to the lungs cause bronchoconstriction

Sympathetic fibres (T2 to T6) dilate the bronchi. Vagal parasympathetic fibres constrict them.
This is why beta-agonists treat asthma.
The cough reflex from the bronchi is mediated by vagal afferents

The cough reflex from the bronchi is mediated by vagal afferents, with cell bodies in the inferior vagal ganglion.
Vagal efferents and phrenic and intercostal nerves produce the cough.

questions.s: Concerning the veins of the superior mediastinum:
o: The arch of the azygos vein passes superficial to the right vagus and deep to the right phrenic nerve

Last's says the arch of the azygos vein passes superficial to the right vagus and deep to the right phrenic nerve, the same relationship as the left superior intercostal vein on the left.
A neat symmetry.
The left superior intercostal vein drains into the left brachiocephalic vein

The left superior intercostal vein drains the second to fourth left spaces and empties into the left brachiocephalic vein, crossing the aortic arch.
It lies between the phrenic and vagus.
In the infant the left brachiocephalic vein may cross the trachea above the jugular notch

In the infant the left brachiocephalic vein may cross the trachea above the jugular notch, relevant to tracheostomy in children.
The thymus is also large then.
The first intercostal space drains into the superior intercostal vein

The first intercostal space drains into the highest (supreme) intercostal vein, which joins the brachiocephalic vein (or vertebral).
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.

questions.s: Regarding the innervation of the oesophagus:
o: The upper striated part is supplied from the nucleus ambiguus

The upper striated part of the oesophagus is supplied from the nucleus ambiguus, via the recurrent laryngeal nerves.
Like the pharynx.
The lower smooth muscle part is supplied from the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus

The lower smooth muscle part is supplied from the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, via the oesophageal plexus.
Like the rest of the gut.
Its sympathetic supply in the upper part comes from the middle cervical ganglion with the inferior thyroid artery

The upper oesophagus receives sympathetic fibres from the middle cervical ganglion along the inferior thyroid artery.
Lower down it gets fibres from the thoracic trunk.
Pain from the oesophagus is carried only by the vagus

Last's says pain from the oesophagus travels with both the vagus and the sympathetic fibres.
So the oesophagus is an exception to the "gut pain is sympathetic" rule.
The jugular notch lies at the level of T3

Last's places the jugular notch at the level of T3 (others say T2/3).
It is the upper border of the manubrium.
The sternal angle lies at the level of T4

Last's gives T4 for the sternal angle (at the T4/5 disc).
It marks the second costal cartilage.
The lower end of the sternum lies at T8

The lower end of the sternum (xiphisternal joint) lies at about T8 to T9.
It marks the lower border of the heart.
The plane of the sternal angle marks the lower limit of the superior mediastinum

The plane of the sternal angle passes back to the T4/5 disc and marks the lower limit of the superior mediastinum.
Many structures begin or end at this plane. All four true: E.

questions.t: Development of the heart and great vessels
o: It is derived from the left sixth arch artery

The ductus arteriosus is derived from the left sixth arch artery. The right dorsal sixth arch artery disappears, so the right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the subclavian.
The left nerve hooks under the ductus.
It closes after birth by contraction of its muscular wall

After birth the ductus arteriosus closes by contraction of its muscular wall, stimulated by the rise in oxygen tension (and fall in prostaglandins).
Anatomical closure follows.
It becomes the ligamentum venosum

The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum.
Arteriosus to arteriosum, venosus to venosum.
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around it

The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around the ductus (ligamentum) arteriosus, lying to its left.
It is at risk in ductus ligation.
